data.content_ref: inline:{"claim": "Two conclusions are the same claim iff they remain equivalent under all counterfactual suppositions the system can generate, i.e., their truth values covary across every hypothetical belief revision.", "mechanism": "The system maintains a set of counterfactual supposition operators. For any pair of conclusions that appear to agree, it systematically supposes the negation of each and checks whether the other is also negated. If they are counterfactually dependent in both directions across all suppositions, they are merged.", "scope": {"covers": ["systems with a well-defined belief revision operator", "conclusions expressible in a language closed under negation"], "excludes": ["conclusions that are not revisable (e.g., axioms)", "systems without the capacity to simulate counterfactual suppositions"]}, "forbidden": [{"case": "Two conclusions are counterfactually dependent under all tested suppositions, but one is a necessary truth and the other is a contingent generalization that happens to be universally true in the system's domain; merging them leads to a false prediction when a novel counterexample to the contingent generalization is encountered.", "eval": "program:counterfactual_merge_failure"}], "prose_notes": "This criterion is strong but computationally expensive. Eager merging risks conflating necessary and contingent truths. Reluctant merging risks maintaining duplicate representations that could be unified, bloating the belief space."}
